Overarching argument: Paul asks whether an industry's year-over-year economic performance predicts its federal political spending (campaign contributions and lobbying), and whether expected partisan control of Congress shapes the amount and partisan direction of that spending. Five initial sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto (crypto analyzed separately). Hypotheses: H1 deep pockets (positive growth effect); H1-alt distress (negative or asymmetric effect); H2 access-seeking (Republican share rises with expected Republican control); H3 stakes (total contributions rise with a toss-up); H4 lobbying tracks current control more than projected control.

works.title: A causal approach for detecting team-level momentum in NBA games
works.summary:
Weimer, Steinert-Threlkeld and Coltin test whether team-level scoring momentum exists in the NBA. Their identification idea is the transferable part. Coach-called timeouts are a response to momentum, so comparing scoring before and after them is biased. TV timeouts fall at points the rulebook fixes, so they act as near-random pauses. The authors take scoring runs of 6 or more unanswered points from 13 seasons (2004-05 to 2016-17) and match runs interrupted by a TV timeout 1:1 on propensity scores to runs with no timeout. In 5,148 matched runs, a TV timeout cuts the running team's points in the next 3 minutes by 11.2% (b = -0.119, about 0.56 points). The effect is larger for longer runs (n = 576 and 48), about 41% smaller when neither team substitutes (n = 4,644), and fades after 3 minutes. A Monte Carlo placebo with zero true momentum returns a null coefficient (b = 0.002, n = 1,336), so the result is not produced by how runs were selected.

None of the basketball findings transfer to Melange, Mentat or Terrier. The method lessons do. First, a treatment someone chooses (a lobbyist's contact, a PAC's spend) is endogenous in the same way a coach's timeout is, so naive before/after or contact-conditioned correlations are biased. Second, a simulated null is a cheap way to show that an estimator or a selection rule does not manufacture effects. The system's prospective receptivity contract already limits its claims to forecasting. The contact-conditioned arm it plans is exactly the coach-timeout design this paper warns against. The engine has no negative control: a repo search of fec/engine for placebo, negative control and null simulation found none.
works.question: Does team-level, in-game momentum exist in NBA basketball, and can a pause in play interrupt it? The test is whether a TV timeout (mandatory, scheduled independently of the game) during a scoring run reduces the momentumed team's subsequent scoring, compared with matched runs that are not interrupted (abstract p.117; Sec. 1 p.118-119).
works.method: Matched observational design with a natural experiment. Propensity-score matching (logistic regression, nearest neighbour; Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983; Ho et al. 2011, MatchIt), with Mahalanobis matching as a robustness check (Table A2, not in text). Outcome: points scored by the momentumed team in the three minutes of game time after the TV timeout (or the run's next play). Estimator: Poisson regression (count outcome, Sec. 4 p.124; Table 3 p.125), with covariates run size and substitutions by each team. Robustness: negative binomial (Appendix B, reported as substantively identical), alternative windows from 60 to 240 seconds (Appendix D), coaches' timeouts as treatment (Appendix E), and a Monte Carlo placebo with zero true effect (Table 5, Fig. 6, p.127-128). Model comparison by bootstrapped AIC, 1,000 resamples of size 48 or 576 (Fig. 3, p.124-126).

findings.finding: A TV timeout during a run lowers the momentumed team's points in the next 3 minutes. Coefficient -0.119 (SE 0.012), p < 0.01, so e^b - 1 = -11.2%. Average gap about 0.56 points.
findings.location: Abstract p.117; Sec. 5.1 p.124; Table 3 col. 1 p.125; Conclusion p.130

findings.finding: Opposing-team substitutions also reduce the momentumed team's scoring, by less than the TV timeout does (about half as strong, per text).
findings.numbers: b = -0.077 (0.017), e^b - 1 = -7.4%; text says TV effect is about 50% larger

findings.finding: Substitutions by the momentumed team have the largest effect in the 6-point model. The authors read this as breaking up the momentumed lineup.
The TV timeout effect grows for longer runs. Opposing-team substitutions lose significance at longer runs.
No mean reversion: the current-run-size coefficient is not significant in any model.
findings.numbers: Text: .001. Table 3 shows -0.002 (0.003), -0.003 (0.009), -0.018 (0.031). The two disagree; see limitations.

findings.finding: The effect is largest right after play resumes. It is about four times as large in the first minute as in the 3-minute window. The 0.56-point figure is therefore a lower bound.
findings.numbers: first-minute effect roughly 4x the 3-minute effect (text)

Blackwell & Yamauchi adjust for unmeasured confounding of strategically placed interest-group ads; Weimer concedes unmeasured strategy changes during timeouts as a limitation. Same strategic-treatment confounding problem.

works.title: Introduction To Monte Carlo Simulation
works.summary:
Harrison (2010) is a short tutorial and history of Monte Carlo simulation. It has no data and runs no simulation. The history runs from Buffon's needle (an intersection probability of 2/pi gives an estimate of pi) through De Forest, Galton and Gosset to von Neumann and Ulam's neutron-shielding work. It then gives a generic recipe: define the model as probability density functions, sample from them repeatedly, and tally the statistics of interest. The paper covers pseudo-random generators (linear congruential generators are poor; it recommends Mersenne Twister), the inversion method, acceptance-rejection, biased table approximation, and normal and Poisson sampling. For the last two it advises using library routines. Its warnings matter most for Paul's systems: simulation gives no exact answers, it is only as good as its model and inputs, it is prone to bugs, and analytic alternatives should be considered first.

The paper is a textbook source, not evidence. It cannot validate any Melange or Terrier parameter. The Melange cascade engines follow the recipe directly: a Bernoulli edge draw u < p on the build_P kernel, a tally of A-coloured activations, and the mean over MC iterations. Terrier's uncertainty draws use the paper's inversion method for categorical cells. The system goes beyond the paper in three ways: it keys draws to individual edges to get common random numbers, it uses splitmix64 and PCG64 generators, and it checks MC stability across seeds. The paper covers none of these. Its main use here is as a caution. The kernel saturation constant 6 and the bystander scale of $400k are unestimated, so the paper's point that simulation is only as good as its inputs applies directly. Its advice to try analytic methods first also supports Paul's wish to test an analytic proxy such as Viral Centrality against the MC cascade. One gap shows up in the code: the scenario and frontier spreads are reported as point means with no Monte Carlo standard error. That finding is UNVERIFIED and rests on a search of four files.
works.question: What Monte Carlo simulation is, where it came from, and how to build one: defining a model as probability density functions, generating random numbers, sampling from standard distributions (uniform, exponential, normal, Poisson), and tallying results. Stated scope: an overview with emphasis on techniques used in medical imaging simulation.
works.method: Narrative review and tutorial. No estimation, no statistical test, no simulation run. Covers: the three-step pattern (p.2); PDF/CDF requirements (p.3); pseudo-RNGs, with LCG (eq. 3) and Mersenne Twister (p.4); inversion method, exemplified by exponential sampling (eqs. 4-6, p.5); acceptance-rejection with steps 1-5 (p.5); piecewise-linear table approximation (p.5); normal sampling via CLT and library routines (pp.5-6); Poisson sampling by counting exponential inter-arrival draws (eq. 8, p.6); tallying recorded events (p.6).

findings.finding: Buffon's needle: for a needle the same length as the line spacing, the probability of intersecting a line is 2/pi. Repeated tosses estimate pi as 2N/X, where X is the number of intersections.
findings.numbers: P = 2/pi; pi estimate = 2N/X

findings.finding: Systematic Monte Carlo was developed during the Manhattan Project by von Neumann and Ulam, to study neutron travel through radiation shielding; the method is named after the Monte Carlo Casino.
findings.numbers: none

findings.finding: Pre-modern simulation examples: De Forest (card deck, mortality tables, 1834-1888); G.H. Darwin (spinner, curve smoothing, 1845-1912); Galton (modified dice for a normal distribution, 1822-1911); Gosset/'Student' (labelled cards, t-test, 1876-1937). Paper calls them seminal but distinct from modern simulation, which solves deterministic problems probabilistically.
findings.numbers: dates only

findings.finding: Simulation drawbacks: it can need huge computing resources, gives no exact solutions, is only as good as the model and inputs, and is prone to software bugs. The author says analytic and experimental alternatives should be considered first.
findings.numbers: none

findings.finding: Weather example: forecasts are more accurate in densely sampled regions (many stations, satellites, balloons) than near poorly sampled regions, so input measurement limits prediction.
findings.numbers: none

findings.finding: A PDF must be non-negative and integrate to 1. The CDF gives the probability that a sampled value is at most x (eq. 2; equation body not extracted).
findings.numbers: integral = 1

It evaluates CELF++ with 50 Monte Carlo simulations per estimate (capturing 11.2% of sampling-based spread), the MC-budget noise evidence that motivates mc_stability_check.py and that Harrison's tutorial does not cover.
It defines the competitive extension of the independent cascade model whose spread the engine estimates with the Monte Carlo recipe Harrison describes.
It states that IC spread is approximated by large Monte-Carlo simulations whose accuracy scales with the number of runs, the computing cost Harrison flags as a drawback.

works.title: On the Use of Two-Way Fixed Effects Regression Models for Causal Inference with Panel Data
works.summary:
Imai and Kim (Political Analysis 29(3), 2021) ask whether the standard linear two-way fixed effects regression (unit plus time dummies) can be read as a design-based, nonparametric causal estimator. Their answer is no. Proposition 1 (PDF p.4) rewrites the 2FE estimator as a matching estimator that builds each counterfactual from three averages: the same unit, the same period, and an adjustment set of size |M_it| x |N_it|. Because that adjustment set includes observations with the same treatment status ("mismatches"), the estimator cannot adjust nonparametrically for unit and time confounders at the same time. Mismatches tend to cause attenuation bias. In the toy example, 2 mismatches in an adjustment set of 4 give K = 3/2 (PDF pp.5-6). The multi-period difference-in-differences estimator, where treatment can switch on and off, equals a weighted 2FE estimator in which some control observations get negative weights (Theorem 1, PDF p.9). The unweighted 2FE estimator equals DiD only in the 2-group, 2-period case. So the causal reading of 2FE depends on the linear additive model, not on the design. The paper is purely analytical: no data, no simulation, binary treatment only. Its software is the R package wfe.

For Paul's systems, this paper bears on one place: the Mentat sector-growth study. That study fits sector-baseline OLS and treats sector+year FE, log-FE and first-difference-with-year-effects variants as robustness checks. On the L-LV lobbying tests the growth slope flips sign under year FE (L3-LV +0.352 to -0.477). The paper explains why this is expected. One-way and two-way FE weight sector-years differently, and the 2FE coefficient is a model-dependent weighted contrast, not a DiD estimate. Sign agreement across those variants is therefore not agreement on a single causal estimand. The DECEL dummy, which switches on and off within each sector, is the paper's exact setting. No other component estimates a causal effect from a panel with unit and time fixed effects.
works.question: Can the linear two-way fixed effects (2FE) regression with unit and time fixed effects be justified as a design-based, nonparametric causal estimator for panel data, both (a) as an adjustment for unit-specific and time-specific unobserved confounders at once and (b) as equivalent to the difference-in-differences (DiD) estimator beyond the two-group, two-period case?
works.method: Algebraic/proof-based analysis. Proposition 1 (PDF p.4): the 2FE estimator (eq. 2) equals a two-way matching estimator with adjustment factor K. Proposition 2 (PDF p.6): a matching estimator using only opposite-status matches equals a weighted 2FE estimator with weights K_it. Section 4: multi-period DiD (eq. 12, PDF p.8) defined via matched sets (eqs. 9-11, PDF p.8) and shown to equal a weighted 2FE estimator with weights W_it (Theorem 1, PDF p.9; proof Appendix A, PDF p.10). Proofs of Propositions 1-2 are in the Online Supplementary Information. No simulation or empirical application appears in the text.

findings.finding: The 2FE estimator can be written as a two-way matching estimator in which each counterfactual is built from the same-unit average, same-time average, minus a pooled adjustment-set average, with a factor K equal to the net proportion of proper (opposite-status) matches.
findings.numbers: Adjustment set size |A_it| = |M_it| x |N_it| (eq. 4, PDF p.4)

findings.finding: Simultaneous nonparametric adjustment for unit-specific and time-specific confounders is impossible under 2FE: mismatches (same-status observations) and an adjustment set containing observations sharing neither the unit nor the time period remain even after restricting to opposite-status matches (Proposition 2).
findings.location: Section 3.2, PDF pp.5-6; Figure 1 caption PDF p.5
findings.numbers: Illustrative example: a_it = 2 mismatches in adjustment set of size 4, so K_it = 1 + 2/4 = 3/2 (PDF p.6)

findings.finding: Under the multi-period DiD design, all three sets (within-unit matched, within-time matched, adjustment) contain only control observations, so mismatches are eliminated.
findings.location: Section 4, Figure 2 and eqs. 9-11, PDF p.8

findings.finding: The multi-period DiD estimator equals a weighted 2FE estimator; the unweighted 2FE estimator is not in general equivalent to it, contrary to common belief.
findings.location: Theorem 1 and text after it, PDF p.9

findings.finding: Some control observations receive negative regression weights, which occurs when (2X_it - 1)(2X_i't' - 1) = -1, i.e., when a control enters the adjustment set for multiple treated observations.
findings.location: Theorem 1 weights and discussion, PDF p.9
findings.numbers: Weight product equal to -1 (no empirical magnitude reported)

findings.finding: The DiD-2FE equivalence holds only in the simplest two-group, two-period setting; with more periods and units switching in and out, the justification of 2FE as DiD requires the linearity assumption.
findings.location: Section 4.2 opening and discussion, PDF pp.8-9
findings.numbers: Two periods, two groups (no numbers)

related.why: Both address causal inference with panel data and time-varying treatments. Blackwell and Yamauchi's IPTW with unit fixed effects in the propensity model for marginal structural models (citing Imai and Kim 2019 on linear FE limits) is a weighting-based alternative of the kind Imai and Kim's conclusion calls for (PDF p.10).

Shares co-author In Song Kim. Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters fit linear probability models with firm, year, politician and firm-politician fixed effects and then a matched DiD (Imai, Kim and Wang), so the FE-panel caveat applies and the matched-DiD step is the design-based route this paper points to.

works.title: The Effect of Political Advertising after Citizens United: Adjusting for Unmeasured Confounding in Marginal Structural Models
works.summary:
Blackwell and Yamauchi (manuscript, 9 Feb 2026) ask whether TV ads run by independent interest groups after Citizens United changed vote shares and turnout. The sample is US Senate and gubernatorial general elections, 2010-2020, measured as weekly media-market by race panels (N = 467 market-races for Democratic-group ads, 623 for Republican). The methods problem is feedback: ads and campaign conditions shape each other, and groups may target persuadable markets on information the researcher cannot see. The authors fit a propensity model with a fixed effect for each unit (estimated by conditional MLE) and use it to build inverse-probability weights for a truncated marginal structural model. They prove root-N consistency when N and T grow together. In simulations (500 replications) the estimator beats IPTW without fixed effects, although some bias remains when heterogeneity is high.

Empirically, Democratic-group ads raise the Democratic two-party share, mostly by raising Democratic turnout, and the effect is concentrated after Trump's candidacy. Republican-group ads show no effect. Placebo tests on lagged outcomes come out near zero. Effects are significant only at alpha 0.1, the text gives no point estimates, and the Trump split is dated 2015 on p.30 but 2016 elsewhere.

For Paul's systems this is mainly a methods paper. It sharpens the caution on Mentat's fixed-effects regressions of sector growth on spending, and it shows a placebo-outcome check that the prospective receptivity contract lacks. It also gives one weak, party-asymmetric data point on Terrier's split between persuasion and mobilization. It says nothing about legislators, so it cannot support the competitiveness multiplier or any part of the flip model's money terms.
works.question: Do independent interest-group TV ads affect Senate and gubernatorial vote shares and turnout after Citizens United, and can an MSM estimator be adjusted for time-constant unmeasured confounding (unit-level heterogeneity) when only a single outcome is observed?
works.method: Proposed IPTW-FE: a two-step procedure. Step 1 fits a parametric logit propensity model with unit-specific fixed effects alpha_i by conditional MLE (incidental-parameters setting). Step 2 builds stabilized inverse-probability weights over the last k+1 periods and solves the weighted MSM estimating equation (weighted least squares for the identity link) (pp.15-17). Theorem 1 gives sqrt(N)-consistency and asymptotic normality with a sandwich variance, with N and T growing at the same rate (p.17); appendix proofs in Appendix A (pp.41-53). Comparators: IPTW with no fixed effects (race-level FE only), and a naive approach that ignores time-varying covariates. Empirical MSM (p.26): E[Y_i(d) | R_i] = gamma_R + gamma_1 * sum_{k=0}^{4} d_{T-k}, race-specific intercepts, effect of one extra week of IG ads in the last five weeks. Weighting model covariates (p.27): lagged Dem poll share and square, undecided/third-party share, Republican negativity over six weeks, cumulative ads by each party and squares, market-race FE. Simulations report bias, SE and 90% CI coverage (pp.22-24).

findings.finding: Democratic IG ads raise the Democratic share of the two-party vote; the effect is driven by a positive effect on Democratic turnout and a weaker negative effect on Republican turnout (per the text; figure values not extractable).
findings.location: Section 6.2, p.28 (Figure 3); Introduction p.4; Abstract p.1
findings.numbers: Coefficients appear only in Figure 3; no point estimates in the text. Results significant at alpha=0.1 per p.30.

findings.finding: Republican IG ads have no estimated effect on any measured outcome.
findings.numbers: No estimate in text; described as null.

findings.finding: The effectiveness of Democratic IG ads is concentrated in the post-Trump era (after 2016 per Abstract and p.5; text on p.30 says 2015). Democratic ads more effective at increasing Democratic votes and reducing Republican votes; differences significant at alpha = 0.1.
findings.location: Section 6.2, p.30 (Figure 4, pp.29-30); Abstract p.1; p.5
findings.numbers: Significance at alpha=0.1; no point estimates in text. Years inconsistent: 2015 (p.30) vs 2016 (p.1, p.5, Figure 4 caption p.29).

findings.finding: Democratic IG ads in the last three weeks show a somewhat stronger positive effect than those 4-5 weeks out; the text calls this consistent with prior experiments.
findings.numbers: Figure 5 only; no numeric values in text.

findings.finding: Magnitudes compared with the literature: Sides et al. (2022) find 0.38-0.87 pp Democratic vote share per 1,000 Democratic-minus-Republican ads; Hewitt et al. (2024) find 1.2-2.3 pp for internal experiments; Klumpp et al. (2016) find 4.1-6.4 pp on House win probability from Citizens United. The authors say their magnitudes are within the broad range and their estimates are slightly higher than Sides et al.
findings.numbers: Sides et al.: 0.38-0.87 pp per 1,000 ads; Hewitt et al.: 1.2-2.3 pp; Klumpp et al.: 4.1-6.4 pp House win probability.

findings.finding: Placebo tests: IPTW and IPTW-FE estimates on lagged (previous-election) outcomes and pre-election Democratic poll share are close to zero; the naive approach shows residual confounding for some Democratic-ad effects.
findings.numbers: Figure 6 only; no numeric values in text.

related.why: Both papers question unit and two-way fixed-effects designs under feedback. Blackwell & Yamauchi cite the 2019 Imai & Kim paper on the same problem. Together they underwrite reading the sector-growth year-FE sign flip as non-causal.
Weimer uses Monte Carlo as a negative control. Blackwell & Yamauchi use placebo outcomes from before treatment. Both are falsification checks that the prospective contract lacks.

Both papers bear on campaign persuasion and its returns, and Broockman co-authored the Hewitt et al. (2024) experiments used here as a magnitude benchmark (1.2-2.3 pp). Together they inform Terrier's split between persuasion and mobilization.

Kalla's experiment identifies the effect of money on legislators' access. This paper identifies the effect of outside spending on voters. The flip model's money assumptions need evidence of the first kind, which this paper does not supply.

works.title: D-NOMINATE After 10 Years: A Comparative Update to Congress: A Political Economic History of Roll Call Voting
works.summary:
Poole and Rosenthal update their 1997 roll-call study through the 105th Congress (1789-1998) using DW-NOMINATE, a dynamic probit spatial model of legislator ideal points. Four results matter here. First, legislator positions are close to fixed over a career: the linear time-trend model adds only about 0.3 points of classification over the constant model (House 85.65 to 85.96; Senate 84.04 to 84.40). Second, Congress has become one-dimensional: the second dimension now adds under 1 percent. Third, party overlap on dimension 1 is near zero: under 1.5% in both chambers over the last five Congresses, and none in the last three Senates. Fourth, polarization rose smoothly, with no break at 1994. A non-parametric rank method produces nearly the same orders (Spearman .960 House, .981 Senate). The donor and primary claim that Paul highlighted in pink rests on a cited working paper that this text does not present.

For the system as built, the paper is a measurement baseline. It is not an engine input. DW-NOMINATE appears only as a control (fec/members/dw_control.py) and through per-Congress Nokken-Poole scores used as a criterion. The sharpest consequence is for the say-do gate's Path V. One CU-aligned final-passage vote counts as corroboration, and in a polarized, one-dimensional chamber that vote mostly records the member's party. A read-only check confirms strong party sorting in several categories (details in bearings). That check is UNVERIFIED. The paper also explains why drift-based susceptibility criteria have little true variance to detect. It argues for using an ideal-point control rather than a bare party dummy wherever party-confounded tiers are interpreted, as in the CFPB isolation. The paper does nothing for lobbying, money effects, pathfinding or allocation.
works.question: Have the trends identified in Congress (1997) toward polarization and one-dimensionality in roll call voting continued through the 105th Congress, and does the 1994 Republican takeover represent a sharp break? Secondary: do DW-NOMINATE and alternative scaling methods recover essentially the same legislator positions, and how does the U.S. Congress fit the spatial model compared with other legislatures? (Abstract p.2; Sec. 1 p.3.)
works.method: DW-NOMINATE (dynamic, weighted, nominal three-step estimation): normal (probit) errors replacing D-NOMINATE's logit errors; per-dimension salience weights w_k; legislator coordinates polynomial in time, estimated as constant (v=0) and linear (v=1) only (p.5-6, Appendix p.19-20). Estimated by maximum likelihood over the joint choice likelihood (eq. A4, p.20). Comparators: Poole's non-parametric optimal classification (rank ordering that maximizes correct classification; one dimension only; Poole 1997, 2000), Heckman-Snyder factor analysis (p.9). Fit measured by percent correctly classified, APRE, and geometric mean probability (Table 1 notes, p.24-25). Party polarization measured by mean within- and between-party pairwise distances (Figs 7-8, p.14) and percent party overlap (Fig 9, p.15). Joint scaling of both chambers estimated with optimal classification (Table 3, p.27).

findings.finding: On Congresses 1-99, 2D linear DW-NOMINATE nearly reproduces D-NOMINATE: correct classification 85.4 (House) and 84.6 (Senate) vs 85.2 and 84.5; dimension-1 coordinate correlations .977 House and .974 Senate; dimension-2 .923 House and .901 Senate.
Adding Congresses 100-105 raises correct classification by about 0.6 points in the House and 0.3 in the Senate; recent Congresses fit the model better than earlier ones.
findings.numbers: House 2D linear 3-Cong: 85.41 (1-99) to 86.08 (1-105); Senate 84.42 to 84.70

findings.finding: The second dimension adds under 2 points of classification in the House and about 2.5 in the Senate over one dimension.
findings.numbers: House 1D constant 83.82 vs 2D constant 85.65; Senate 81.46 vs 84.04

findings.finding: The linear (time-varying) model is not a striking improvement over the constant model; lowering the linear threshold from 5 to 3 Congresses adds about 0.1 (House) and 0.3 (Senate) points.
findings.numbers: House 2D constant 85.65 vs linear 85.96 (5-Cong threshold) and 86.08 (3-Cong); Senate 84.04 vs 84.40 and 84.70; about 0.3 points for linear over constant

findings.finding: Unidimensionality trend: the second dimension now adds under 1 percent of improvement over the first in both chambers; the authors call the post-early-1970s trend dramatic.
findings.location: Sec. 3, p.7-8 (Figs 1B, 2B are not in the text)
findings.numbers: under 1 percent

findings.finding: Utility-function estimates for DW-NOMINATE: second-dimension salience weight w-squared is .3160 (House, linear) and .3087 (Senate, linear); beta is 4.125 (House, 2D linear) and 4.078 (Senate, 2D linear). Standard errors are acknowledged as not econometrically correct.
findings.numbers: w^2 .3160 House, .3087 Senate; beta 4.125 House, 4.078 Senate (2D linear)

related.why: Aref and Neal partition signed House co-sponsorship networks (1981-2017) and find the optimal 2-partition and especially the 3-partition leave fewer frustrated edges than the party partition, with a fluid third coalition. NOMINATE dim1 is a natural benchmark for whether those members are more than near-center moderates.
Earlier optimal signed partition of House and Senate co-sponsorship networks (sessions 96-114); its coalitions can be checked against DW-NOMINATE ideal points.
Bonica estimates candidate and contributor ideal points from contribution records and compares them with DW-NOMINATE; relevant to the donors-and-primaries claim this paper leaves unevidenced.
A formal model (no data) of how presidential going-public can raise legislative polarization; a mechanism for the polarization trend this paper measures.

works.title: Optimal Targeting in Fundraising: A Causal Machine-Learning Approach
works.summary:
Cagala, Glogowsky, Rincke and Strittmatter ran a natural field experiment in 2014 with a Catholic Church fundraiser in one German city (N=19,779 church members). A small gift (postcards, cost 1.16 euro) was randomly assigned with the solicitation letter, stratified by warm list (past donors, N=2,354) and cold list (never donors, N=17,425). Sending the gift to everyone barely paid for itself on the warm list (net +0.06 euro, not significant) and lost money on the cold list (-0.97 euro per person). Gift effects varied widely across warm-list donors, from -11.59 to +17.99 euro between the 5th and 95th percentiles. The authors used AIPW scores and a depth-2 exact policy tree (Athey-Wager policy learning) to learn who should get the gift. Under 20-fold cross-validation, the rule sent the gift to 33% of the warm list and raised expected net donations by about 2.1-2.2 euro (about 14%) over all-gift, no-gift and random assignment. On the cold list the rule chose almost nobody (1.4%). Geospatial covariates alone did about as well as the full set of covariates. Applied to a new 2015 sample, the rule only helped where the 2015 donors closely resembled the 2014 donors (caliper match 0.1). On the full 2015 sample it showed no significant gain.

What this means for Paul's systems: a targeting rule for a costly treatment is only justified when it beats uniform and random benchmarks out of sample, and that requires randomized variation in the treatment. Melange's money allocators and Terrier's canvass potential score both target on heterogeneity that is assumed, through hand-set response curves, multipliers and weights. Neither is learned from a randomized assignment. The paper describes the experiment and benchmark test the system lacks. It does not validate any of the system's constants. Its setting (individual charitable donors) also differs from the system's targets: legislators for Melange, and voters for Terrier.
works.question: Can a charity raise more net donations (donations minus fundraising cost) by targeting an unconditional gift (small Dürer postcards mailed with a solicitation letter) to a subset of potential donors, using causal machine learning to learn an optimal targeting rule from a randomized field experiment, and does that rule generalize? Theory: charities face costly fundraising and donor overhead aversion (Rose-Ackerman 1982; Name-Correa and Yildirim 2013; Gneezy et al. 2014); the optimal rule targets "net donors" whose expected additional donation exceeds the marginal cost; heterogeneous motives (altruism, warm glow, reciprocity, sequential reciprocity) make gift effects heterogeneous across individuals.
works.method:
Potential-outcomes framework. CATE delta(x) and ATE identified under stratified randomization and SUTVA (Appendix B). Outcome-model/propensity nuisance estimation: logit for propensity, OLS for outcome regressions (Table D.1), combined into an augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) score (Eq. 3-4). Optimal targeting rule estimated directly via Athey and Wager (2021) empirical welfare maximization, using exact policy-learning trees of Zhou, Athey and Wager (2018) with search depth two (policytree R package). Gains evaluated by 20-fold cross-validation of out-of-sample net donations versus all-gift, no-gift and random-gift benchmarks. Descriptive heterogeneity: sorted-effects approach (Chernozhukov, Fernandez-Val and Luo 2018) with multiplier-bootstrap bands, plus best linear predictor test with causal forest (Chernozhukov et al. 2020). Data-type ablations (socioeconomic, donation history, geospatial, combinations). Sensitivity to depth one and three exact trees, CART (fixed and cross-validated depth), weighted logit (baseline and flexible), logit lasso, classification forest; nuisance robustness via population propensity and cross-fitted lasso (Tables I.1-I.4). Identification of the targeting gain does not require identifying the causal effect of each characteristic; trees indicate correlations only.
Identification strategy: random assignment of the gift within strata (Zi), exogenous of potential outcomes conditional on Zi, 0 < p(z) < 1; heterogeneity variables Xi are not needed for identification.

findings.finding: Gift ATE on donations (first year): warm list +1.21 to +1.24 euro, not significant. Net of the 1.16 euro gift cost: +0.05 to +0.08 euro, not significant. Cold list ATE +0.19 euro (significant); net of cost -0.97 euro per donor, so the all-gift rule loses money in the cold list.
findings.numbers: warm ATE 1.21-1.24 (SE 1.15-1.25); warm net 0.05-0.08; cold ATE 0.19 (SE 0.07-0.10); cold net -0.97 (SE 0.07-0.10); preferred AIPW warm ATE 1.22, net 0.06

findings.finding: Heterogeneity: sorted effects show substantial individual variation in warm-list gift effects; 45% of warm-list individuals have estimated effects above the 1.16 euro cost. Effects range from +17.99 euro (95th percentile responders) to -11.59 euro (5th percentile). In the cold list, effects exceed cost only above the 92nd percentile and are small.
findings.numbers: warm: 45% above cost; 5th pct -11.59 euro; responsive individuals +17.99 euro; cold: 5th pct -0.73, 95th pct +1.38 euro

findings.finding: Best linear predictor test with causal forest detects significant effect heterogeneity in the warm list and none in the cold list.
findings.location: Section 5.2 and Table E.3 (p.21; Appendix p.12)
findings.numbers: warm heterogeneity loading 0.959* (SE 0.710); cold 0.511 (SE 1.069)

findings.finding: Warm list optimal rule (cross-validated out-of-sample): gift is assigned to 33% of warm-list individuals; expected net donations 17.61 euro, which is 2.14 euro (13.8%) above all-gift, 2.20 euro (14.3%) above no-gift, and 2.17 euro (14.1%) above random-gift, all significant.

findings.finding: Secondary outcomes (warm list): donation probability in first year is +0.025 (significant at 5%) vs no-gift, with no significant difference from the all-gift rule; net donations over two years are 32.94 euro, +2.33 vs all-gift and +3.75 vs no-gift, so the gains persist and there is no evidence of pull-forward.

Expected net donation 0.15 euro, essentially equal to no-gift (-0.005, not significant), and significantly above all-gift (0.97 euro) and random-gift (0.48 euro). The paper concludes the gift should not be sent to cold-list individuals at all.
findings.numbers: share treated 0.014; net donation 0.15***; vs all-gift 0.97*** (0.10); vs no-gift -0.005 (0.012); vs random 0.48*** (0.05)

Item file title matches Simchon et al. 2024 on persuasive effects of political microtargeting; it parallels the policy-tree vs all-gift comparison in persuasion.

works.title: Validating the Applicability of Bayesian Inference with Surname and Geocoding to Congressional Redistricting
works.summary:
DeLuca and Curiel test Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) against the race people reported on their own voter-file records. They use the North Carolina and Georgia voter files, Black versus White only, with ZIP-level priors from zipWRUext. They compare two ways of turning each voter's posterior into precinct and district totals. One sums the probabilities (PSM). The other gives each voter the most probable race and counts those (plurality or modal assignment, PM). Across 10,000 simulated congressional plans per state, PSM had lower absolute error in nearly every district. Under PSM the Black share was off by at most about 5 points in both states. The White share was off by about 0 points in North Carolina and up to about 10 in Georgia. At the precinct level, PM had a longer right tail of errors, especially for Black voters. The authors expect errors of 5 to 10 points at the district level. They expect errors to be largest where surnames carry little information and areas are mixed. Their results come from two highly segregated states with two dominant groups.

None of the Melange federal components estimate race, and none aggregate individual probabilities to areas, so most of the system has no bearing here. The paper matters for Terrier. Terrier's row framework already follows the PSM rule. It takes expected values over imputed class probabilities and never the most probable class (argmax). Area top-decile shares are built from summed probabilities, not flags. This paper is the first outside evidence in the vault for that rule, which was owner policy with no literature behind it. The exposed spot is the Luna completion step, which fills each blank with the most probable class. That is exactly the PM rule the paper argues against. If the area measures read those filled codes, they are plurality aggregates. The transfer is about how to aggregate, not about race. It holds best when the class probabilities are reasonably calibrated, and it is UNVERIFIED for vendor consumer fields until an area-level holdout check exists.
works.question: Can Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) estimate the racial composition of precincts and congressional districts accurately enough for redistricting, and which posterior allocation rule is better: summing probabilities (PSM) or plurality/modal assignment (PM)? (Abstract p.465; Intro pp.465-466.)
works.method: Descriptive validation against ground truth. (1) Run BISG with zipWRUext and form two allocations: PSM (sum posteriors within a precinct) and PM (assign each voter to the modal race). (2) Precinct check: compute absolute percentage difference between BISG-estimated and reported counts for White and Black voters, shown as density plots (Fig. 1, p.466-467). (3) District check: draw 10,000 congressional plans per state with the Redist package v2 using rook contiguity on the precinct base map. For each plan, compute absolute percentage-point difference between BISG-estimated and voter-file share for each race, then take the distribution and a 95% interval (p.467). Results are plotted against district White or Black population share (Fig. 2, p.468).

findings.finding: PSM significantly reduces error rates at the precinct and district level relative to plurality assignment; recommended as the preferred method for BISG in redistricting (abstract).
findings.numbers: not reported as a single number

findings.finding: Precinct level: for White voters the modal error approaches zero under both methods, but PM has a longer right tail. For Black voters PSM vastly outperforms PM.
findings.numbers: qualitative; no point estimates in main text

findings.finding: District level: in nearly all district estimates, PSM gives significantly lower absolute error than PM across 10,000 simulated plans per state.
findings.numbers: 10,000 plans per state; 95% CIs plotted

findings.finding: North Carolina, PSM: White-share error close to zero; Black-share error never above 5 percentage points.
findings.numbers: White about 0 pp; Black max 5 pp

findings.finding: Georgia, PSM: White-share error reaches about 10 percentage points; Black-share error is lower and peaks around 5 percentage points.
findings.numbers: White max about 10 pp; Black peak about 5 pp

findings.finding: Headline district-level accuracy: PSM district minority-share estimates typically fall within five percentage points of voter-file race, with error varying by state and group.
findings.numbers: typically within 5 pp

related.why: Real item (American Politics Research 2022 on commissions and partisan gerrymanders). Link is thin: DeLuca supplies a racial-composition measure, and no direct analytic dependency was checked. Weak link.
Real item on the gameability of redistricting criteria. Both papers are in redistricting. The shared ensemble-of-plans method was not verified in Becker and so the same-method label is withdrawn.

works.title: Is Bigger Always Better? Potential Biases of Big Data Derived from Social Network Sites
works.summary:
Hargittai asks whether people choose social network sites at random. They do not. In the 2013 Pew national survey (N = 1,801; regression N about 1,510-1,528), age, education, income, gender and race each predict use of Facebook, LinkedIn and Twitter. For example, the LinkedIn coefficient on logged income is 0.72 and on high school or less is -1.37. In a panel of UIC students (2009 to 2012, regression N about 517-519), 2009 Internet skills and use frequency predict which sites people adopted by 2012 (skills to Tumblr 0.62, Twitter 0.33). Adoption differs widely by site (2012: Facebook 89%, Twitter 38%, LinkedIn 18%). Her conclusion is that data from one site describe that site's users only. A biased sampling frame can reverse the direction of a finding, not just add noise. Studies should state their frame in the title, abstract and results.

**What this means here.** Legislators are elite accounts, so platform adoption bias mostly disappears on X: 502 of 515 members in social_media.db have an X handle. It comes back on Bluesky. Bluesky posts run 2023-07-01 to 2026-09-19. Of the 533 roster members (259 D, 271 R, 3 I), 135 posted on Bluesky: 117 D, 16 R and 2 I. Of the 411 Bluesky member-to-member mentions, 392 are D to D, and none cross party. These mentions are added at weight 0.4 to the social interaction layer, which enters the live augmented cascade network. The second problem is the media blend: a member silent on social media in a category gets half their press signal, so silence counts as zero stance. Both counts are my own reading of live files. They stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062). The paper's coefficients do not carry over to this system. Only its sampling-frame logic does.

works.title: The Gameability of Redistricting Criteria
works.summary:
Becker and Gold take two common redistricting criteria, preserving counties and changing the prior plan as little as possible, and show that each can be measured in many defensible ways. The measures disagree about which map is best. On a hand-built 24x24 grid, Plan 2 splits the fewest counties (1), Plan 3 has the lowest Shannon split entropy (1.265) and Plan 4 has the best Even Splits score (2.485). In a 10x9 grid example, the plan that ties for the lowest People Change (9.5%) has the second-worst Area Change (13.3% against a best of 7.8%). On Minnesota (11 maps) and Wisconsin (6 litigation maps), no map is best on both a county-split measure and a least-change measure. Two Minnesota plans move almost the same share of people (1.90% and 1.93%), yet their incumbent-people change is 13.90% against 1.93%. The paper's verdict is that a vague criterion lets each party pick the metric its own map wins on. Its recommendation is to define metrics explicitly but avoid hard numeric caps. The analysis is descriptive only, with no inference. It used relaxed population balance (up to 1%) and precinct or ward units, and the study was funded by Jenner & Block.

The paper has no bearing on the influence engine, stance, SNA or Mentat. Its relevance is narrow: the system's district-geography plumbing. That code compares old and new congressional boundaries (CD116 vs CD119 in `redistricting_density.py`, and the CBP/ACS vintage mismatch in the census scraper) and orients Cook PVI across the mid-decade redistricting. In both places the system uses single, implicit change measures: whether the seat label changed, a weighting based on block counts, and a state-list flag plus a PVI-shift flag. The paper shows that this kind of choice decides the answer. Its weaker, general lesson, that choosing a metric reorders the winners, also applies to the score blend's three weight sets, which are unratified and documented inconsistently. Everything in this note is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
works.question: How should 'preserve subdivisions' (county splitting) and 'least change from a prior district plan' be measured, and do different defensible measures rank the same maps differently, so that the criteria can be gamed by choosing a metric?
works.method: Descriptive metric comparison (no inference). Section 4 defines county-split measures in four families: count-based (counties split, unnecessarily split, total county parts, split-county parts, unnecessary split-county parts, total county fragments), boundary-based (intra-county cut edges, and their length), entropy-based (Shannon entropy, Even Splits score, Square Root Entropy) and weighted variants. Section 5 defines least-change measures in matching-based form (People, Area, Precinct change), matching-free boundary forms (common-refinement perimeter, symmetric-length and symmetric-cut-edge perimeter), pairing forms (incumbent-people, incumbent-precinct, precinct-pair change), and Fowlkes-Mallows and Variation of Information. Each measure is computed on hand-built grid plans with worked arithmetic. Minnesota and Wisconsin plans are scored on all measures. Computer-generated Minnesota plans come from local search using ReCom and flip moves (DeFord-Duchin-Solomon 2021; Fifield et al. 2020), each run to maximize or minimize one metric. This search is not representative sampling. Plans 1-5 in Table 1 were hand-designed to illustrate properties, not produced by the optimizer (fn.4 p.12).

findings.finding: Different county-split metrics pick different best plans on the same grid set. Plan 2 has the fewest counties split (1), Plan 3 has the lowest Shannon entropy (1.265) and fewest intra-county cut edges (18), and Plan 4 has the lowest Even Splits score (2.485) and fewest total county fragments (11).
findings.numbers: Counties split: P1=3, P2=1, P3=2, P4=2, P5=2, P6=5, P7=9. Shannon: P3=1.265 best. Even Splits: P4=2.485 best. Intra-county cut edges: P3=18 best.

findings.finding: The most compact grid plan (Plan 6, designed to maximize compactness) splits the most counties apart from Plan 7. The paper says plans designed to preserve counties do better across the board.
findings.numbers: Plan 6: 48 cut edges (lowest), 5 counties split, 16 total county parts. Plan 7: 154 cut edges, 9 counties split.

findings.finding: Worked sample plan (Fig. 2, 24x24 grid, 4 districts of 144): splits 3 counties (C2, C5, C7); 12 total county parts; 14 total county fragments; 34 intra-county cut edges; Shannon entropy about 1.821; Even Splits about 4.804.
findings.numbers: 3 counties split; 12 parts; 14 fragments; 34 intra-county cut edges; Shannon 1.821; Even Splits 4.804.

findings.finding: Change metrics pull apart. On the grid balanced variants, Plan 2 ties Plan 3 for best People Change (9.5%), while Plan 1 has the best Area Change (7.8%). The text says Plan 2 has the second-worst Area Change.

Minnesota: the court-ordered 2022 map is not the best on any measure but is 'far from the worst'. Plans 7-10 were built to do well on change measures, and the best change scores are spread across four plans.
findings.numbers: Court-ordered: 9 counties split, 99 total county parts, Shannon 7.84, People change 7.50%, Area change 13.07%. Best change scores: Plan 8 People 1.93%, Plan 7 Precinct 1.09%, Plan 10 Area 0.28%.

findings.finding: Population-based and incumbency-based change can diverge sharply. Plan 8 and Plan 9 move almost the same share of people, but Plan 9's incumbent-people change is far worse because an incumbent's precinct moved. The text says Plan 9 moves 0.03% more people than Plan 8; Table 3 shows the reverse (1.90% vs 1.93%), so this is an internal inconsistency to verify.
findings.numbers: Incumbent-people change: Plan 8 = 1.93%, Plan 9 = 13.90%. People change: Plan 8 = 1.93%, Plan 9 = 1.90% (table) vs text '+0.03%' for Plan 9.

related.why: Both evaluate redistricting plans. Best et al. ask whether commissions avoid partisan gerrymanders; Becker and Gold show that procedural criteria such as county splits and least change can be gamed through metric choice. Item file title confirmed.

Both concern congressional district geography at block or precinct level. DeLuca and Curiel validate Bayesian surname-and-geocoding inference for congressional redistricting; the link is measurement validity for district-level inputs, not change metrics.

A 2024 Cook Political Report ratings piece in the same input family as the Cook district PVI that drives COMPET_MULT. The link is conceptual only: Becker and Gold measures say how far a district moved, which governs whether a PVI value carries over. Report content was not checked here.

The dataset could matter for one component. It treats a seat as structural CU power and never asks how the member came to hold it. Paul flags a chicken-or-egg problem between partisanship and committee selection. works.title: An introduction to grf
works.summary: A 2026 tutorial vignette for the grf R package (Sverdrup, Hadad, Athey, Tibshirani, Wager), not a research paper. It walks through causal forests for conditional average treatment effects, AIPW doubly robust average effects, best linear projection (BLP) of effect heterogeneity on covariates, rank-weighted average treatment effect (RATE) via TOC/AUTOC curves to test whether a prioritization rule actually concentrates the treatment effect, Qini curves for budgeted targeting, and depth-limited policy trees learned from doubly robust scores. Two randomized examples: a Brazilian school financial-education RCT (about 17,000 students, 850 schools; ATE 4.35 points, SE 0.52; whole-sample AUTOC p = 0.65, but prioritizing low financial autonomy gives AUTOC 0.69, SE 0.22) and a payday experiment (about 2,500 people; held-out AUTOC 0.0061, SE 0.0092, no heterogeneity). The authors flag that out-of-bag TOC tests are heuristics without finite-sample guarantees and that policy trees need held-out evaluation. For Paul's systems the value is methodological. Every targeting score he ships (Terrier untapped potential, the Melange PERS persuadability table, receptivity seed_prob) is a hand-built or correlational ranking of who is most movable. grf supplies the standard test of whether such a ranking sorts people by treatment effect rather than by outcome level. None of it transfers without logged treatment assignment (randomized or known-propensity canvass contacts, outreach or money) and outcomes, which none of the systems currently record. Observational use assumes unconfoundedness. Any analysis built on this stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.
works.question: Not a research paper: a tutorial showing how to use the grf R package for heterogeneous treatment effect (CATE) estimation, doubly robust ATE, best linear projection, TOC/AUTOC evaluation, Qini policy evaluation and interpretable policy learning.
works.method: causal_forest with W.hat and clusters; average_treatment_effect (AIPW); best_linear_projection with HC3 cluster-robust SEs; out-of-bag CATE predictions; rank_average_treatment_effect for TOC/AUTOC; variable_importance; double_robust_scores and policy_tree depth-1 for interpretable policies; regression_forest for nuisance Y.hat; maq sister package for Qini and budget policies (described, not run). Tutorial only, no new estimator.

Best linear projection on financial.autonomy.index: coefficient -0.0329 (SE 0.0128, p = 0.0099); students with higher autonomy benefit less (p.7).
Other BLP terms: is.female -0.7268 (SE 0.5307, p = 0.17); family.receives.cash.transfer -1.1992 (SE 0.6526, p = 0.066); is.unemployed 0.3206 (SE 0.6277, p = 0.61) (p.7).
Whole-sample AUTOC using out-of-bag predictions: one-sided p = 0.65, so no reliable heterogeneity signal overall; authors call the evidence suggestive only (p.8).
TOC prioritizing low financial autonomy: AUTOC estimate 0.69, SE 0.22, t about 3.2; bottom 20 percent by autonomy have ATE about 1.1 points above average with CI excluding zero (p.9).
Depth-1 policy tree: assign training if financial.autonomy.index is 41 or below (p.10). Double robust mean scores: control 58, treated 62 (p.9).
