works.title: Various Versatile Variances: An Object-Oriented Implementation of Clustered Covariances in R
works.summary: Zeileis, Koell and Graham (JSS 95(1), 2020; reprint run on sandwich 3.1-3) describe the sandwich package's object-oriented clustered and panel covariances: vcovCL (one-way and multi-way, HC0-HC3, G/(G-1) adjustment, odd/even inclusion-exclusion with an optional multi0 swap), vcovPL (panel Newey-West and Driscoll-Kraay), vcovPC (Beck-Katz PCSE) and vcovBS (clustered bootstrap). Worked examples reproduce multiwayvcov, plm and pcse to six decimals on the Petersen benchmark. On the Aghion et al. hurdle model, clustered SEs come out roughly 1.5 to 2 times the basic sandwich SEs. The Monte Carlo (10,000 replications, clusters of 5) finds CL-0 coverage near 0.95 across lm, GLMs, beta and count models once G is around 50 to 100. At G = 10, standard errors are underestimated, and the order from best to worst is HC3, HC2, HC1, HC0. The bootstrap is only somewhat better than HC0 and HC1 at that size. Panel NW and PCSE fail when panels are short or the dependence is exchangeable rather than decaying. The main relevance to Paul's systems is the Mentat sector growth study. Its two-way sector-by-year CR1 sensitivity in sgs_review.R is Equation 20 of this paper, implemented by hand. Its primary inference clusters by 5 to 9 sectors. That is below the paper's smallest tested G of 10, a size the paper already shows to be anti-conservative for CR1-type errors. The study's choice of a wild cluster restricted bootstrap with Webb weights, rather than CR1 t-tests, is therefore the right instinct. However, this paper does not test WCR bootstrap-t (its vcovBS is a variance bootstrap), so it neither validates nor refutes that choice. The SEATS-W test treats Newey-West HAC as secondary with no p-value, which matches the paper's finding that panel NW is unreliable. The paper has no bearing on networks, lobbying identity or allocation.
works.question: How can clustered and panel sandwich covariances be provided as one object-oriented R implementation that works for any model with estfun() and bread() methods, and how well do these covariances perform in finite samples beyond lm() and glm()?
works.method: Object-oriented sandwich estimators in R package sandwich: vcovCL (one-way and multi-way clustered covariances with HC0-HC3 bias corrections, cluster factor G/(G-1), multi-way inclusion-exclusion sum with odd/even signs, optional multi0 variant), vcovPL (panel Newey-West and Driscoll-Kraay with Bartlett or other kernels, lag NW1987 or NW1994), vcovPC (Beck and Katz panel-corrected SEs, balanced and unbalanced via pairwise or casewise), vcovBS (clustered bootstrap with xy, residual, wild, Mammen, Webb, norm types, R default 250). Benchmarks against lmtest, multiwayvcov, plm, geepack, pcse and lme4 random-intercept models, and GEE with exchangeable correlation.
findings: Sec 5.1 (p.17): hurdle negbin on Aghion et al. data with CL clustering by company (803 clusters): institutions in zero part 0.00658, clustered SE 0.00209, p = 0.0016; in count part 0.00397, SE 0.00430, p = 0.357. Only the zero-part coefficient is significant.

Sec 5.1 (p.17-18): usual standard errors greatly overstate precision. Standard and basic sandwich SEs for zero institutions are both about 0.00135 versus 0.00209 under clustering; clustered SEs are about 1.5 to 2 times the basic sandwich SEs.
Sec 5.1 (p.18): the clustered bootstrap (vcovBS, R = 250) agrees closely with CL-1, e.g. count institutions 0.00411 versus 0.00430, at much higher computational cost.

Sec 5.2 (p.18-19): on the Petersen benchmark (500 firms, 10 years), one-way firm-clustered slope SE 0.050596 from vcovCL matches multiwayvcov; plm and geepack give 0.050540 with HC0 and no cluster adjustment.
Sec 5.2 (p.20): two-way firm and year clustering gives intercept SE 0.065066 and slope SE 0.053561 (multi0 = TRUE); the authors caution that year has only 10 clusters, below what theory requires.

Sec 5.2 (p.20-21): Driscoll-Kraay vcovPL with adjust = FALSE gives slope SE 0.028163, identical to plm vcovSCC; PCSE slope SE 0.025276 agrees with pcse, including unbalanced panels (pairwise 0.025338, casewise 0.025241).

related.why: The paper cites Zeileis 2006b for the object-oriented sandwich framework that vcovCL and vcovPL extend. Verified in the reference list and Sec 3.
The paper cites Zeileis 2004 for the HC and HAC estimators reused in vcovPL and the HC0-HC3 corrections (text ~line 336 and ~line 773). Verified.

works.title: Object-Oriented Computation of Sandwich Estimators
works.summary: Zeileis (JSS 16(9), 2006; read as the sandwich package vignette) recasts heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC) and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) covariance estimation as a modular sandwich S = (1/n) B M B, where the bread B is the inverse Hessian and the meat M is the variance of the empirical estimating functions. R generics bread(), estfun(), meat(), meatHC() and meatHAC() let one computation serve lm, glm, survreg and other models. Two illustrations show what the correction does. In a Poisson fit to simulated negative-binomial data (n = 250), the naive z for I(x^2) is -2.12 (p = .034); with the sandwich it is -1.35 (p = .18). In a probit on Fair's affairs data (n = 601), age moves from p = .033 to p = .051. The author's own caveat carries the most weight: sandwich errors help only if the point estimates stay consistent, they cost power when the model is right, and the package does no inference itself. For Paul's systems the paper is a method source, not evidence. The Mentat sector-growth study hand-codes the same estimators in base R: HC1 (meat as an outer product with the n/(n-k) factor) as a reference-only error, CR1 and two-way cluster errors, and, in SEATS-W, a Bartlett-weighted Newey-West HAC at 2, 4 and 8 week lags kept secondary with no p-value. The way the system is built already follows the paper's caveat, since primary inference comes from wild-cluster and block bootstraps. The paper's HC meat also ignores cluster dependence, which the study handles separately with CR1. One real gap: HC1 and CR1 are cross-checked against statsmodels in a test, but no comparable second-path check was found for the hand-coded HAC (for example against sandwich::NeweyWest), so under DE-062 those HAC numbers stay UNVERIFIED.
works.question: How can sandwich (robust) covariance matrix estimators be computed in general parametric models fitted by estimating functions, not only in lm(), so that inference such as partial z or t tests is robust to some model misspecification.
works.method: Object-oriented R infrastructure in the sandwich package: generics bread() (default Hessian-based bread, Eq. 9, p.5), estfun() (n x k matrix of empirical estimating functions, p.6), meat() outer-product estimator (Eq. 10, with optional n/(n-k) adjustment, p.6), meatHAC() with weights over lags (Eq. 11, p.7), meatHC() with diagonal omega(r, hat, df) (Eq. 12, p.8), and sandwich() = (1/n) B M B (p.8-9). Wrappers vcovHAC(), vcovHC(), kernHAC(), NeweyWest(), weave(). Inference via lmtest coeftest() and waldtest(), car linear.hypothesis(). Methods are demonstrated for glm (poisson, quasipoisson, glm.nb), survreg via tobit(), and glm probit.
findings: Sandwich form S = B M B with M = VAR[psi] and B = inverse expected Hessian (Eq. 4-6, p.2-3); estimator is S-hat = (1/n) B-hat M-hat B-hat (p.8-9).
Poisson fit on overdispersed NB data: naive z-test of I(x^2) is -2.12, p = 0.034; sandwich SE 0.0363 gives z = -1.35, p = 0.18 (Sec 5.1, p.10-11).
Quasi-Poisson gives the same conclusion: I(x^2) SE 0.0506, z = -0.97, p = 0.33; glm.nb gives coefficient -0.0527, SE 0.0649, z = -0.81, p = 0.42 (p.11).
Poisson coefficients track the true conditional mean (intercept 1.0633, x 0.9961, true values 1 and 1); only dispersion is misspecified (p.10).

Tobit on Fair's affairs (n = 601): HC SEs only slightly differ from model SEs; religiousness SE 0.4038 vs sandwich 0.3999; rating -2.2850 with SE 0.4078 vs sandwich 0.3935; age SE 0.0791 vs sandwich 0.0889 (p.12).
Tobit: age p-value moves from 0.0234 to 0.0437 with sandwich, still significant at 5 percent; occupation remains insignificant (0.200 vs 0.185) (p.11-12).

related.why: Real item. The 2006 text cites Zeileis 2004 JSS 11(10) as the linear-model predecessor, and the 2004 text covers HC4 and Andrews-type HAC weights, matching the claim that this paper only cites those details.
Real item. Its title is an object-oriented implementation of clustered covariances in R, which is the CR extension of the same bread and meat framework that the growth study uses via CR1.

works.title: Econometric Computing with HC and HAC Covariance Matrix Estimators
works.summary: Zeileis (JSS 11(10), 2004; reprinted as the sandwich package introduction) is a software paper, not an empirical study. It casts HC and HAC covariance estimators as one sandwich form, (X'X)^-1 X'Omega X (X'X)^-1, and gives R tools that plug into coeftest and structural-change tests: vcovHC (const, HC0-HC4, HC3 default) and vcovHAC with Newey-West, Andrews kernel and Lumley weights, optional VAR prewhitening and automatic bandwidth. Three worked examples carry the numbers. On 50 US states (1979 school spending), the quadratic income term goes from SE 830 (HC0, p .056) to SE 5489 (HC4, p .77) because one high-leverage state, Alaska, drives it. On the Greene investment series, three HAC settings move the RealGNP SE from 0.0168 to 0.0236 (about 40 percent) without changing the conclusion. On quarterly US real interest 1961-1986 (103 quarters), a HAC-scaled CUSUM rejects stability (p .0082) and Bai-Perron dating finds breaks in 1972(3) and 1980(3). There is no simulation evidence. Claims about small-sample performance come from Long and Ervin (2000) and Cribari-Neto (2004). For Paul's systems this is a method source for the robust-variance rows in Mentat. The forecast refit calls sandwich::vcovHC HC1 and vcovCL directly. The SEATS-W weekly test hand-codes a Bartlett Newey-West SE at fixed lags 2, 4 and 8 weeks and labels it secondary. The paper's own examples support that design: HAC lag and prewhitening choices visibly move SEs. Its leverage example qualifies the HC1 rows in small refit regressions (df about 11). Nothing here touches the network, lobbying or influence components.
works.question: How to turn HC (heteroskedasticity-consistent) and HAC (heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent) covariance estimators from the econometrics literature into reusable, modular computational tools in R that plug into fitted models and inference procedures.
works.method: Estimator functions in R package sandwich: vcovHC(lmobj, omega, type = HC3 default) for HC; vcovHAC(lmobj, weights, prewhite, adjust, sandwich, order.by, ar.method, data) for HAC. Weight helpers: NeweyWest (Bartlett with lag L, default data-driven bwNeweyWest), weightsAndrews and bwAndrews via kernHAC (default quadratic spectral kernel, VAR(1) prewhitening, AR(1) bandwidth), weightsLumley via weave (truncate C=4 or smooth C=1). Inference: coeftest from lmtest with z tests (df = Inf) or t tests; gefp and sctest for OLS-based CUSUM with kernHAC; Fstats for supF; breakpoints (Bai and Perron 2003 dynamic programming, BIC-chosen partition) with confint using vcov = kernHAC.
findings: Public schools (Sec 4.1, p.10-11): HC0 gives the quadratic income term I(Income^2) coefficient 1587, SE 830, z 1.91, p 0.056 (weakly significant); HC4 gives SE 5489, z 0.29, p 0.77 (clearly non-significant).
The HC0 vs HC4 difference is attributed to a single high-leverage outlier, Alaska (Figure 2, p.11), with HC4 correcting for leverage.

Investment (Sec 4.2, p.11-13): RealGNP coefficient 0.1691 is significant under all three HAC variants: SE 0.0168 (Newey-West lag 4, no prewhitening, p<2e-16), SE 0.0236 (Newey-West automatic bandwidth with prewhitening, p 7.4e-13), SE 0.0208 (Parzen kernel, VAR(2) prewhitening, no finite-sample adjustment, p 4.7e-16).
RealInt coefficient -1.0014 is not significant under any of the three HAC variants: SE 3.3424, 3.6399, 3.9475 with p 0.76, 0.78, 0.80 respectively (p.12-13).

Intercept under the three HAC variants: SE 18.9583, 24.3742, 24.6639 (p 0.51, 0.61, 0.61) (p.11-13). Paper states the three estimators give slightly different standard errors but agree on the substantive conclusions.

Real interest CUSUM (Sec 4.3, p.13-14): OLS-based CUSUM with quadratic spectral kernel HAC variance (VAR(1) prewhitened, AR(1) bandwidth) crosses its 5 percent boundary; sctest p = 0.0082, indicating a significant change in mean with a clear peak in the early 1980s.

related.why: The paper points to Zeileis 2006b, Object-Oriented Computation of Sandwich Estimators, as the follow-up implementation. The rel's claim that it generalizes to any model with estimating functions and bread was not confirmed in this paper's text, so the link rests on the paper's own citation.

Later work by Zeileis, Koll and Graham on clustered covariances in the same sandwich package. This 2004 paper does not cite it, so the link is real but is not a citation from this paper. The vcovCL use in the Mentat refit is a code fact, not something this paper supports.

works.title: Difference-in-Differences with a Continuous Treatment
works.summary: Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (arXiv 2107.02637v8, 2025) work out what difference-in-differences identifies when treatment comes as a continuous dose rather than an on/off switch. Under ordinary parallel trends, only effects for the units that actually got dose d are identified (ATT(d|d), and ATT_loc pooled over treated units). Comparing outcomes across dose levels mixes the causal response with a selection-bias term (Thm 3.2). Causal responses such as ACRT(d), the derivative in dose, need strong parallel trends: the response to each dose must be the same across dose groups. Pre-period data cannot test that assumption. The common two-way fixed effects (TWFE) dose-by-post slope is a weighted average with non-obvious weights. In the levels form those weights integrate to zero and are negative below the mean dose (Thm 3.4). The slope also depends on the dose units and on whether untreated units are included. In the Medicare PPS hospital application (5,881 hospitals, 1980-1986), TWFE gives 1.14. That sits near ATT_loc = 0.80 only because two biases offset. ACRT_glob = -0.08 (s.e. 0.19), and dropping untreated units shrinks TWFE by 78 percent while the causal responses do not move. Estimation uses binarized DiD plus B-spline sieve regressions with honest uniform bands. The paper bears most on the Mentat sector-growth regressions, which put a continuous growth measure into sector-plus-year fixed-effects models with no zero-dose group. It also bears, as a design template, on the open question of whether money's effect is concave, which the Melange money terms assume but never estimate. Purely econometric. No lobbying, network or legislator content.
works.question: How should difference-in-differences designs with a continuous or multi-valued dose be identified, interpreted and estimated? Which causal parameters are identified under standard parallel trends versus stronger assumptions, and what does the common two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression with a dose-by-post interaction actually estimate?
works.method: Two-period DiD with continuous dose, identified under parallel trends (PT, Assumption PT) and strong parallel trends (SPT, Assumption SPT). Estimators: (i) binarized DiD regression of the outcome change on an indicator for positive dose (eq 4.6), which recovers ATT_glob under SPT; (ii) saturated regression with dose dummies for discrete doses (eq 4.1); (iii) quadratic parametric regression among treated units (eq 4.2); (iv) nonparametric sieve regression with cubic B-splines and a data-driven Lepski-type sieve dimension (Chen, Christensen and Kankanala 2025), with honest uniform confidence bands (Appendix B). ACRT_glob is the sample mean of estimated ACRT(D_i) over treated units. TWFE is decomposed (Theorem 3.4) into causal response, levels, scaled levels and scaled 2x2 representations with explicit weights (Table 1). Extensions: staggered timing (Appendix C), relaxing SPT through bounds, sub-regions and covariate-conditional SPT (Sec 5). Pre-trend checks use event-study versions ATT_loc(e) and ACRT_loc(e). Inference clusters at the hospital level.
findings: Under PT, ATT(d|d) and ATT_loc = E[dY|D>0] - E[dY|D=0] are identified (Thm 3.1, p.10). The main text makes clear that ATT(d) is not identified under PT alone.
Under PT alone, comparing outcome paths across dose groups mixes a causal response with a selection bias term ATT(l|h) - ATT(l|l); causal responses are not identified (Thm 3.2, p.11).
Under SPT, ATT(d), ACRT(d), ATT_glob and ACRT_glob are identified; ACRT_glob equals the average derivative weighted by the dose density among treated (Thm 3.3, Cor 3.1, p.12-14).
The TWFE coefficient is a weighted integral of ATT(d|d) whose weights integrate to zero, with negative weights below the mean dose and positive above (Thm 3.4(b), p.16-17).

Under PT, the TWFE causal-response decomposition is a convex average of ACRT(d|d) plus selection bias, with positive weights integrating to one (Thm 3.4(a), p.16). Positive weights do not make TWFE a natural target.
Equation 3.1 writes beta_twfe as a Wald-type ratio with distance weights; in the application the numerator is 0.60 and the denominator 0.53 (p.17, p.28).

related.why: Imai and Kim (Political Analysis 2021) critique two-way fixed effects with panel treatments; this paper gives the continuous-dose analogue of that caution. Item exists and is linked to the same sector-growth component.

Covers the wild cluster bootstrap inference layer the sector-growth study uses with few clusters; this paper covers what the point estimate means, not inference. Item exists; MacKinnon text not re-read here.

Kalla and Broockman (AJPS 2016) is a randomized field experiment on whether contributions buy access, the experimental counterpart of the observational money dose-response design discussed here. Confirmed from the item's paper record.

The grf vignette is an introduction to generalized random forests for heterogeneous effects; this paper points to Neyman-orthogonal and double machine learning routes for ACRT_glob as future work (p.22). Item exists; grf text not re-read here.
The money_response.py calibration comment cites Ansolabehere for the small MAXSHIFT, so the link is real in the code. The Ansolabehere paper text was not re-read here.

works.title: The Bipartisan Path to Effective Lawmaking
works.summary: Harbridge-Yong, Volden and Wiseman ask whether bipartisanship pays for individual lawmakers. They use all House and Senate members in the 93rd-114th Congresses (1973-2016; about 9,000 House and 2,170 Senate legislator-Congress rows) and regress the Volden-Wiseman Legislative Effectiveness Score on the share of a member's cosponsors who come from the other party. The design uses legislator fixed effects. That attracted share predicts effectiveness: within member, the coefficient is 0.433 in the House and 0.330 in the Senate, so one SD is worth about 6-8 percent of mean LES. The share members offer to the other party's bills does not predict effectiveness once controls are in. The effect holds across eras, majority margins and polarization levels, and in majority and minority strata. It is an inverted U that peaks near a 50/50 cosponsor mix (0.496 House, 0.512 Senate). In the House the attracted share also predicts each later stage, from committee action to law. Offering cross-party cosponsorships predicts attracting them, at 0.317 within member in the House and 0.547 in the Senate. The evidence is observational, with one-tailed tests and no design-based identification. For Paul's system, the sharpest point concerns direction. bpf is an undirected, symmetrized cross-party tie share. Cooperation v2's directional component measures offered support. Nothing in the system measures attracted support, which is the side the paper ties to effectiveness. The flip model's (1+0.3 bpf) passage bonus and the coalition seed boost (1+0.8 bpf) are monotone, but the paper finds a peak and then a decline. The paper's reciprocity is cosponsorship exchange. It does not validate the money reciprocity in D-104..D-108. Any transfer is UNVERIFIED until it is reproduced on Paul's data.
works.question: Why does bipartisanship persist in Congress despite polarization and primary threats? The paper asks whether legislators who attract a larger share of opposite-party cosponsors on their bills are more effective at advancing them, whether that holds across eras and party conditions, whether the effect has an optimum, and whether offering bipartisan cosponsorships in turn drives attracting them (reciprocity).
works.method: Cross-sectional time-series least squares regressions with legislator fixed effects and robust standard errors (Tables 1-3, A2-A13); pooled OLS and fixed-effects OLS for reciprocity regressions (Table 4, clustered SEs in pooled models). Nonlinear models add a squared term. Robustness: commemorative-bill exclusion, normalization by Congress, cosponsorship-level controls, low-cosponsorship eras, binary alternative measures, Lugar index, no member FE, electoral safety interactions, later legislative stages, hitchhiker-inclusive law counts, and era splits (pre/post 1994).
findings: Table 1 Model 1.2 (House, p.17): proportion bipartisan cosponsors attracted = 0.433 (SE 0.097), p<0.001; Model 1.5 (Senate, p.17) = 0.330 (SE 0.147), p<0.05. One SD increase = +0.08 LES in House and +0.06 in Senate, about 6-8 percent of mean LES of 1.0 (p.16).

Uncontrolled Models 1.1 (House 0.986) and 1.4 (Senate 0.538) are larger; the coefficient on proportion bipartisan cosponsorships offered is not significant with controls (Model 1.3 = -0.234; Model 1.6 = -0.420) (p.17-18).
Robust to excluding commemorative bills, normalizing by Congress, controlling for cosponsorship levels, binary alternative measures (Table A5 House 0.213, p<0.001) and the Lugar index (p.18-19).
Without member fixed effects coefficients are larger (Table A6 with controls: House 0.552, p<0.001; Senate 0.440, p<0.001) (p.18-19, Appendix p.10).

Table 2 (p.20-21): effect stays positive and significant (House 0.432 to 0.629; Senate 0.358 to 0.442) when interacted with a Congress counter, majority margin or party polarization; all interactions small and not significant.

Table 3 nonlinearity (p.22-23): House linear 1.828 and squared -1.844 peak at 0.496; Senate 1.666 and -1.626 peak at 0.512. A one-SD decline costs about 22 percent of LES in House and 16 percent in Senate; a one-SD rise adds about 8 and 4 percent (p.24).

related.why: Sotoudeh (2024) measures cosponsorship influence on House bill passage and contrasts it with the Volden-Wiseman LES. This paper uses LES as its outcome.
Battaglini, Leone Sciabolazza and Patacchini model LES as a Katz-Bonacich centrality of the cosponsorship network. This paper uses the cross-party composition of cosponsors instead.
Bucchianeri, Volden and Wiseman extend the Volden-Wiseman effectiveness framework to American state legislatures (SLES).
Aroyehun (2026) also regresses Congressional LES on a member-level predictor, emotional expression from floor speeches. The link is a shared outcome, not shared data.

Aref and Neal (2021) partition House cosponsorship signed networks; their third coalition, marked by negative same-party ties, is the most effective coalition in most sessions. Their coalitions are signed-network partitions, not cross-party by definition.

works.title: Wild Bootstrap Inference for Wildly Different Cluster Sizes
works.summary: MacKinnon and Webb (Queen's WP 1314, corrected 2019; JAE 2017) study when cluster-robust (CRVE) t tests with t(G-1) critical values give correct size, and when the wild cluster bootstrap does better. Using Monte Carlo designs with 50 or 100 clusters sized like U.S. states (4 to 242 observations), CPS placebo laws (547,518 obs, 51 states) and a Colombian replication, they show the rule of 42 fails once cluster sizes are unequal: t(G-1) rejects up to 0.107 at nominal .05 with 50 state-sized clusters and 0.084 even with 100. The restricted wild cluster bootstrap (WCR) stays near .05 in those designs (0.049 to 0.053). The bootstrap breaks when few clusters are treated: with one treated cluster of 50 the t(G-1) test rejects 77.75 percent of the time while the WCR never rejects; WCR is safe roughly for 7 <= G1 <= G-7 with equal clusters and 6 <= G1 <= G-5 with unbalanced clusters at G of 20 to 32. The effective-clusters G* correction is erratic. Rademacher weights are not advised below about 12 clusters. For Paul's systems the paper is the method source for one component: the Mentat sector growth study already runs a WCR bootstrap-t by sector with Webb six-point weights, enumerating all 6^G draws when small, and labels per-sector terms resting on one cluster DESCRIPTIVE, which matches the paper's G1 = 1 warning. The open point is scale: the study runs with 3 to 9 sector clusters, below the 12-cluster floor of every design the paper tests, so the paper supports the procedure choice but does not certify its size at G = 9 or 5. No network, lobbying-edge or influence claim follows.
works.question: When is inference with cluster robust variance estimator t statistics (CRVE, with t(G-1) critical values) reliable, and which alternatives (effective number of clusters G* critical values, restricted or unrestricted wild cluster bootstrap) work when cluster sizes are very unequal or the number of treated clusters is small?
works.method: Monte Carlo rejection frequencies at nominal .05 (and .10 and .01 in places) for: CRVE t with t(N-2), t(G-1), t(G*-1) and t(G*) critical values (G* at rho = 0.99 and rho-hat); restricted wild cluster bootstrap (WCR) with symmetric P values; unrestricted bootstrap (WCU, Appendix A.3); HCCME t with normal critical values. Rho-hat from the cluster-dummy regression. Power comparison of micro versus aggregate estimators (Appendix A.8) with bootstrap tests.
findings: Section 4, Table 1 (p.6): with 50 equal-sized clusters, t(G-1) rejection rises with the regressor's within-cluster correlation and exceeds 0.065 when rho_x is 1 (value 0.06568 at rho_eps 0). Wild bootstrap rejections in Tables 1 and 3 all lie close to .05 (Table 1 range 0.04924 to 0.05084, p.8).

Section 4, Table 2 (p.7): with 50 state-sized clusters (sizes 4 to 242), t(G-1) rejection is 0.05784 with both correlations zero and reaches 0.10718 at rho_eps 0.9 and rho_x 1 (text says 0.1073, a small mismatch with the table). Bootstrap rejections range 0.04905 to 0.05277 (p.10).

Section 4 (p.10): with state-sized clusters, t(G*-1) critical values underreject severely when rho_x is large; worst case rejection 0.0166 at rho_eps 0 and rho_x 0.6, where average G* is 9.43 using rho-hat and 5.97 using rho 0.99.

Section 4, Table 4 (p.9): with 100 state-sized clusters (each state appearing twice), t(G-1) rejection reaches 0.08442 (rho_eps 0.9, rho_x 1); the wild cluster bootstrap never exceeds 0.05124. The rule of 42 fails under unequal clusters even at 100 clusters.

Section 5, Figure 1 (p.11): for DiD with t(G-1) critical values, severe overrejection when G1 (treated clusters) or G minus G1 is near 0; with equal-sized clusters rejection is near .05 for G1 from 17 to 34. Overrejection is worse when the smallest clusters are treated first.

Section 5, Figure 2 (p.12): t(G*-1) critical values overreject except when the number of treated clusters is very small or very large; extreme underrejection at G1 = 1 and G1 = 49. Figure 3 (p.13): restricted wild bootstrap underrejects severely when G1 or G minus G1 is very small but works extremely well for G1 from about 7 to 43 (equal-sized clusters).
